title: Thinking and Working Scientifically: Investigations, Variables, Tables and Graphs
kicker: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint · Science 0097 · Stage 6 · Working scientifically
summary: How to plan a fair test, name the variables, measure accurately, record results, draw the right graph, spot anomalous results, write conclusions and improve an investigation — the skills that appear in almost every Checkpoint question.

blocks.text: Almost every Checkpoint Science question has a part about **how science is done**: naming a variable, completing a table, reading a graph, finding an odd result or suggesting an improvement. These marks are easy to win once you know the rules on this page.

items: variable
متغيّر — anything that can change in an investigation
independent variable
المتغيّر المستقل — the one thing YOU change
dependent variable
المتغيّر التابع — the thing you MEASURE or observe
control variables
المتغيّرات الثابتة (المضبوطة) — things you keep the SAME
fair test
تجربة عادلة — only one variable is changed
prediction
توقّع — what you think will happen, with a reason
hypothesis
فرضية — a scientific idea that might explain something and can be tested
hazard / risk
مصدر خطر / خطر — something that could cause harm / how likely harm is
reliable
موثوق — you get similar results when you repeat
accurate
دقيق — close to the true value
anomalous result
نتيجة شاذة — a result that does not fit the pattern

المتوسط الحسابي — add the values, divide by how many

blocks.text: 1. Scientific questions and the five types of enquiry

A **scientific question** is one you can answer by collecting evidence. "Which is the most beautiful rock?" is not scientific (it is an opinion). "Which rock soaks up the most water?" is scientific — you can test it. Once you have a question, choose the **type of enquiry** that can answer it.

rows: You change ONE variable, measure another and keep all the others the same.
Does the temperature of water affect how fast sugar dissolves?
You watch the same thing and record changes at regular times (minutes, days, months).
How does the shape of the Moon change over a month?
You cannot control the variables, so you collect data from many people, places or things and look for a link.
Do taller children have longer arm spans?
You sort things into groups by their features, often using a key.
Is this rock igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic?
You use secondary sources to answer questions you cannot test (too big, too far, too slow, too dangerous, or about the past).
How do fossils of sea animals end up on mountains?

blocks.text: **How to choose:** Can you change one thing and keep everything else the same? → fair test. Is it about change over time? → observing over time. Is it about many living things or places that you cannot control? → pattern seeking. Are you sorting or naming? → identifying and classifying. Can you not test it yourself? → research.
2. Models and diagrams

A **model** represents something real so that we can understand it. Models are useful when the real thing is **too small** (particles), **too big or too far** (the Solar System), **hidden inside the body** (heart and lungs), or **too slow** (the rock cycle). A diagram is a kind of model.

headers: How it is different from the real thing (its limits)
rows: Balls in a box for particles
Particles in a solid are close and in rows; in a gas they are far apart and move fast.
Real particles are far too small to see and they are not coloured balls.
A ball and a lamp for the Moon and Sun
Why the Moon seems to change shape: we see different amounts of its lit half.
Sizes and distances are completely wrong.
Two balloons in a bottle for the lungs
Air goes in when the space in the chest gets bigger.
Real lungs are not hollow bags; they have millions of tiny air sacs.
Who eats whom, and how energy passes along.
It does not show how many of each animal there are.

blocks.text: In the test you may be asked to **use** a model ("draw the particles", "draw the force arrows", "complete the circuit diagram") or to say **how a model helps** ("it shows … that we cannot see") and **one way it is not like the real thing**.
3. Predictions and hypotheses

A **prediction** says what you think will happen **and why**, using science you know. A good prediction has two parts: **I predict that … because …**. A **hypothesis** is the scientific idea behind it — an explanation that can be tested.

items: Weak: "I think the sugar will dissolve." (no comparison, no reason)
Good: "I predict that sugar will dissolve **faster in hotter water**, **because** the water particles move faster and break up the sugar more quickly."
In a new (unfamiliar) context, still use science: "I predict the plant in sandy soil will wilt first, because sand does not hold much water."

blocks.text: 4. Variables and fair tests
In a **fair test** you change **only one** variable, so you know that it caused any difference in your results.

rows: the time for the sugar to dissolve
volume of water (100 ml); mass of sugar (5 g); type of sugar; stirring (same number of stirs); same type of beaker

items: Write the independent variable as "the ___ of the ___" (the temperature of the water) — never just "the water".
The dependent variable is usually something you read from an instrument: a time, a distance, a temperature, a mass.
For control variables, name a **quantity**, and if possible give its value: "the same volume of water, 100 ml".
If a question says "Why is it a fair test?", answer: "Only one variable (the ___) was changed; everything else was kept the same."

blocks.title: المتغيرات بسهولة
blocks.text: المتغيّر المستقل = الحاجة اللي أنا بغيّرها بإيدي. المتغيّر التابع = الحاجة اللي بقيسها (وقت، مسافة، درجة حرارة). المتغيّرات الثابتة = كل حاجة تانية لازم تفضل زي ما هي عشان التجربة تبقى عادلة. واكتب دايمًا "the temperature of the water" مش "the water" بس.
5. Risks and safety
A **hazard** is something that could cause harm (hot water, glass). A **risk** is the chance that harm happens. Before practical work, describe each risk and say how to **minimise** it.

headers: How to make the risk smaller
rows: An adult pours it; keep beakers on a heatproof mat in the middle of the table; do not carry hot water around
Hold them carefully; lay a thermometer so it cannot roll; tell the teacher about breakages; do not pick up glass with your fingers
Keep the area clear; stand to the side
Wear gloves; wash hands with soap afterwards

blocks.text: **Exam tip:** name the hazard AND the action. "Be careful" earns nothing. "Hot water could burn you, so let an adult pour it" earns marks.
6. Choosing equipment and measuring accurately

rows: mm, cm, m (km for long distances)

blocks.text: Choose equipment with a **suitable scale**: use a 100 ml measuring cylinder (not a bucket) for 50 ml of water; use a stopwatch, not a wall clock, for a 10-second time. Then read it carefully:

items: Work out what **one small division** is worth (count the gaps between two numbers).
Read with your **eye level** with the reading (for a liquid, the bottom of the curved surface, called the meniscus).
Start a ruler at **0**, not at the edge of the ruler. Set a balance to **zero** before adding the object.
Write the value **and the unit**.

blocks.text: 7. Units you must know
The prefixes tell you the size: **milli (m) = one thousandth**, **centi (c) = one hundredth**, **kilo (k) = one thousand**.

rows: area of a rectangle = length × width
millilitre (ml), litre (l), cubic centimetre (cm³), cubic metre (m³)
weight is a force, so it is measured in N
water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C

blocks.text: To change a big unit into a small one, **multiply** (2.5 kg = 2.5 × 1000 = 2500 g). To change a small unit into a big one, **divide** (350 cm = 350 ÷ 100 = 3.5 m).
8. Repeating measurements

Measurements are rarely exactly the same each time (you press the stopwatch a bit late, the car leaves the ramp slightly differently). **Repeating** a measurement (usually three times) and working out the **mean** makes the data **more reliable**. Repeat when results vary a lot, when a result looks odd, or when the measurement is quick and easy to get slightly wrong (like timing).
**Mean** = add the values ÷ how many values. Leave out any anomalous result before you work out the mean.
9. Sorting, classifying and using keys

We can **sort and classify** objects, materials and living things by **testing** (Does a magnet attract it? Does it let electricity through?), by **observing** (Does it have legs? Is it shiny?) and by using **secondary information** (a book says whales breathe with lungs, so they are mammals, not fish). A **key** is a set of yes/no questions about features that are easy to see. Each question splits the group in two until each thing has its own name.

items: Use features you can **see** (legs, shell, colour, wings), not ones you cannot ("Is it fast?", "Is it dangerous?").
Each question must have only **two** answers (yes / no).
When you complete a key, check that every living thing ends in its own box.

blocks.text: 10. Secondary sources

**Secondary sources** are information that someone else collected: books, reliable websites, encyclopaedias, videos from science organisations, data tables, or an expert (a doctor, a farmer, a geologist). Use them when you cannot test something yourself.

items: Use **more than one** source and check that they agree.
Check **who** wrote it (a science organisation, a museum or a university is more reliable than an advert or a random post) and **when** (is it up to date?).
Pick only the evidence that is **relevant** to your question, and write it in your own words.

blocks.text: 11. Recording results in tables

items: Put the **independent variable** in the **first column**, in order (20, 40, 60).
Put the **dependent variable** in the next columns, with a column for each repeat and one for the mean.
Write the **unit in the heading** (in °C, in s), not after every number.
Use a ruler and give every column a heading.

blocks.text: Check the means: (118 + 122 + 120) ÷ 3 = 360 ÷ 3 = 120; (75 + 78 + 75) ÷ 3 = 228 ÷ 3 = 76; (50 + 47 + 47) ÷ 3 = 144 ÷ 3 = 48. For some enquiries a labelled **diagram** is better than a table — for example, drawing the Moon's shape each night.
12. Choosing the right chart or graph

rows: distance a car rolls on carpet, sand, wood, tiles
both variables are **numbers** and the independent variable can take any value (or it is time)
time to dissolve at 20, 30, 40… °C; temperature every minute
you measure **two things about many individuals** to look for a pattern (pattern seeking). Points are NOT joined.
height and arm span of 10 children
you want to show **how often** each value appears
number of peas in each of 12 pods

blocks.text: **Drawing a graph:** independent variable on the **x-axis** (across), dependent on the **y-axis** (up); label both axes with the **unit**; choose a scale that goes up in equal steps and uses most of the grid; plot points as small crosses in pencil, exactly; draw bars of equal width with gaps for a bar chart.
13. Patterns, anomalous results and conclusions

Describe a pattern with **"As … increases, … increases / decreases"**, then add numbers from the data. From the line graph: "As the temperature of the water increases, the time for the sugar to dissolve **decreases** — from 120 s at 20 °C to 48 s at 60 °C."

An **anomalous result** does not fit the pattern (80 s at 50 °C should be about 60 s). It may be caused by a mistake: the timer started late, the sugar was not stirred, or less hot water was used. What to do: **repeat** that measurement, and leave it out of the mean and the line.

A **conclusion** answers the question of the investigation and explains it with science: "Sugar dissolves faster in hotter water, **because** the particles of water move faster and break up the sugar more quickly." Then compare with your **prediction**: "My prediction was correct: I said hotter water would dissolve sugar faster, and the time went down from 120 s to 48 s." If only part of the prediction was right, say which part.

blocks.title: النتيجة الشاذة والاستنتاج
blocks.text: النتيجة الشاذة (anomalous) هي النتيجة اللي مش ماشية مع باقي النتايج. بنعيد القياس ده، وما بندخلهوش في حساب المتوسط. والاستنتاج لازم يرد على سؤال التجربة ويقول السبب العلمي بكلمة because.
14. Evaluating and improving an investigation
To **improve** an investigation, say **what** to change and **why** it helps:

rows: Repeat each measurement three times and work out the mean
Results are more reliable; odd results can be spotted
"One spoon" of sugar (spoons can be fuller or emptier)
Measure 5 g of sugar on a balance each time
Keeps a control variable really the same, so the test is fairer
Test more temperatures, e.g. every 10 °C from 20 °C to 70 °C
The pattern is clearer; you can see where an odd result is
Stir every beaker the same number of times
Only the temperature changes — a fair test

blocks.text: Worked examples
**Worked example 1** (variables)

Mona investigates how the mass of plasticine on a paper boat affects how deep the boat sinks into water. She adds 10 g, 20 g, 30 g and 40 g of plasticine and measures how far the boat sinks below the water surface.
(a) Name the independent variable. [1]
(b) Name the dependent variable. [1]
(c) Name two variables Mona must keep the same. [2]

items: (a) What does Mona change? → **the mass of plasticine** (on the boat).
(b) What does she measure? → **how deep the boat sinks** (the distance below the water surface).

(c) Things that could also change the result: **the same paper boat (size and shape)**, **the same type of paper**, **the same water (type and depth)**, **plasticine put in the same place on the boat**. Any two = 2 marks.

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** writing "the plasticine" for (a). Say what about it changes: its **mass**.
**Worked example 2** (prediction and its accuracy)

Before the dissolving investigation (line graph above), Sami predicted: "Sugar will dissolve faster in hotter water."
(a) Add a scientific reason to Sami's prediction. [1]
(b) Was his prediction correct? Use the results to explain. [2]

items: (a) "… **because the particles move faster** in hot water."
(b) Yes, the prediction was correct [1]: the time to dissolve went down as the temperature went up, from 120 s at 20 °C to 48 s at 60 °C [1].
A full answer can also mention that the result at 50 °C did not fit and should be repeated.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3** (repeats, anomalous result and mean)
Ali times how long an ice cube takes to melt in three places. He repeats each one three times.
(a) Which result is anomalous? [1] (b) Work out the mean for the classroom table, leaving out the anomalous result. [1] (c) Why did Ali repeat each measurement? [1]

items: (a) **27 min** — the other two classroom results are 19 and 20, so 27 does not fit.
(c) To make the results **more reliable** / to spot an anomalous result.

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** dividing by 3 after leaving out a value. You only added two values, so divide by 2.
**Worked example 4** (choosing a graph and describing a pattern)

(a) Yara measured the distance a toy car rolled on four surfaces. Which type of graph should she draw? Give a reason. [1]
(b) Describe the pattern shown in the scatter graph of height and arm span. [1]

items: (a) A **bar chart**, because the type of surface is a word (category), not a number.
(b) **As height increases, arm span increases** (taller children have longer arm spans).

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** (risks)
Ahmed uses water from a kettle at 60 °C in glass beakers. Describe one risk and how to reduce it. [2]

items: Risk [1]: hot water could **scald / burn** his skin (or: the glass beaker could break and cut him).
Action [1]: an **adult pours** the hot water / keep the beaker on a heatproof mat away from the edge (or: handle glass carefully and report breakages).

blocks.text: **Worked example 6** (improving an investigation)
Sara added "one spoon of sugar" to each beaker and timed each beaker once. Suggest one improvement and explain why it helps. [2]

items: Improvement [1]: measure the **same mass of sugar (for example 5 g) with a balance**. Why [1]: spoons hold different amounts, so this keeps a control variable the same and makes the test fair.
Or: **repeat** each temperature three times and calculate a mean [1], because this makes the results **more reliable** [1].

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Mixing up independent (change) and dependent (measure). Say: "I change the independent; I measure the dependent."
Writing vague variables: "the water" instead of "the temperature of the water" or "the volume of water".
Writing "to make it fair" as the reason for repeating. Repeating makes results **reliable**; keeping control variables the same makes the test **fair**.
Drawing a line graph for categories (words) — use a bar chart.
Joining the points on a scatter graph.
Including an anomalous result in the mean, or dividing by the wrong number.
Reading a scale without working out what one small division is worth.
Forgetting the unit, or using kg for weight (weight is in newtons, N).

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: "Name the variable that … changes / measures / keeps the same." — use the exact words from the question.
"Write a prediction" — use "I predict … because …".
"Complete the table" — copy values exactly; add the mean; headings need units.
"Circle the anomalous result" or "Which result does not fit the pattern?" — compare with the other repeats or with the line.
"Describe the pattern" — "As … increases, … increases/decreases", with two numbers from the data.
"Suggest one way to improve" — WHAT to change + WHY it helps (two marks).
"Read the thermometer / measuring cylinder" — find the value of one small division first.
"Which type of enquiry?" — fair test, observing over time, pattern seeking, identifying and classifying, research.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Working scientifically: practice
blocks.intro: 14 questions in the Checkpoint style, from easy to hard. Use a calculator if you need one.

questions.q: Nour wants to find out how the height of a sunflower changes over six weeks. Which type of scientific enquiry should she use?
questions.e: She records the same plant changing over a period of time — observing over time.

questions.p:
Question 2
Adam investigates how the height of a ramp affects how far a toy car rolls along the floor. He releases the car from the top of the ramp at heights of 10 cm, 20 cm and 30 cm and measures how far it rolls.
ans: height of the ramp in cm
questions.e: The independent variable is the one Adam changes: the height of the ramp.

questions.p:
Question 2
Adam investigates how the height of a ramp affects how far a toy car rolls along the floor. He releases the car from the top of the ramp at heights of 10 cm, 20 cm and 30 cm and measures how far it rolls.
questions.e: The dependent variable is what he measures: the distance the car rolls.

questions.p:
Question 2
Adam investigates how the height of a ramp affects how far a toy car rolls along the floor. He releases the car from the top of the ramp at heights of 10 cm, 20 cm and 30 cm and measures how far it rolls.
questions.q: (c) Name two variables Adam must keep the same to make it a fair test.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, any two: same car / same mass of car; same floor surface; same ramp (length, material, surface); release the car without pushing / from the same point at the top; measure the distance in the same way (e.g. from the bottom of the ramp to the front of the car). Do not accept: height of the ramp (that is the independent variable); distance (dependent variable); "same everything".
questions.e: Anything else that could change how far the car rolls must stay the same, for example: the same car, the same floor surface, the same ramp, letting go without pushing, measuring from the same point.

questions.q: Read the temperature shown on the thermometer.
questions.e: Between 0 and 10 there are 10 small marks, so each small mark is 1 °C. The red liquid ends 7 marks after 30: 30 + 7 = 37 °C.

questions.q: A bag of rice has a mass of 2.5 kg. What is its mass in grams?
Hana measures how long a sugar cube takes to dissolve in water, milk, tea and orange juice. Which type of graph should she use to show her results?
questions.e: The independent variable (type of drink) is a word, not a number, so she should draw a bar chart.

questions.p:
Question 8
Rami times how long a paper spinner takes to fall 2 m. He drops it four times. His times are: 3.2 s, 3.0 s, 4.7 s, 3.1 s.
questions.q: (a) Which time is the anomalous result?
questions.e: 3.2, 3.0 and 3.1 are all close together. 4.7 s is much bigger, so it does not fit the pattern: it is anomalous.

questions.p:
Question 8
Rami times how long a paper spinner takes to fall 2 m. He drops it four times. His times are: 3.2 s, 3.0 s, 4.7 s, 3.1 s.
questions.q: (b) Work out the mean time, leaving out the anomalous result.
questions.e: Leave out 4.7 s. 3.2 + 3.0 + 3.1 = 9.3. There are 3 values: 9.3 ÷ 3 = 3.1 s.

questions.q: In which unit is weight measured?
questions.e: Weight is a force, and forces are measured in newtons (N). Mass is measured in kg or g.

questions.p:
Question 11
Use this key to identify four animals: a pigeon, an ostrich, a tilapia fish and a camel.
1  Does it have feathers?  Yes → go to 2.   No → go to 3.
2  Can it fly?  Yes → pigeon.   No → ostrich.
3  Does it have fins?  Yes → tilapia.   No → camel.
questions.q: An animal has no feathers and no fins. Use the key to name it.
questions.e: Question 1: no feathers → go to 3. Question 3: no fins → camel.

questions.q: Laila wants to find out how quickly hot water cools in cups made of different materials. She will pour water at 80 °C into cups made of glass, plastic and metal. Describe one risk and say how she can reduce it.
questions.ms: 1 mark for a risk: hot water could scald / burn the skin; OR glass could break and cut. 1 mark for a matching action: an adult pours the hot water / keep cups on a heatproof mat / do not carry or move full cups / let the water cool before tipping it away; OR handle glass carefully / tell the teacher about breakages / do not touch broken glass. Do not accept: "be careful" on its own.
questions.e: Example: "The hot water could burn her skin, so an adult should pour it and the cups should stay on a heatproof mat in the middle of the table."

questions.p:
Question 13
Salma pours 200 ml of water at 80 °C into four cups made of different materials. After 10 minutes she measures the temperature again.
metal cup: 45 °C   glass cup: 55 °C   plastic cup: 62 °C   polystyrene cup: 74 °C
questions.q: Write a conclusion for Salma's investigation.
questions.ms: 1 mark: the polystyrene cup kept the water warmest / the water cooled least in polystyrene / polystyrene is the best (thermal) insulator. 1 mark: the metal cup let the water cool the most / metal is the best (thermal) conductor; OR a correct order: polystyrene, plastic, glass, metal (from best to worst at keeping heat in). Accept ora (reverse argument).
questions.e: The water in the polystyrene cup stayed hottest (74 °C), so polystyrene is the best thermal insulator. The water in the metal cup cooled the most (45 °C), so metal is the best thermal conductor and lets heat escape fastest. From best to worst at keeping water hot: polystyrene, plastic, glass, metal.

questions.q: Kareem measured the time for a ball to roll down a slope only once for each slope. Which change would make his results more reliable?
c: use a bigger ball for each slope
repeat each measurement and calculate a mean
use a different slope each time
write the results in a list instead of a table
questions.e: Repeating measurements and taking the mean makes results more reliable. Changing the ball or the slope would make the test unfair, and how you write results does not make them more reliable.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Independent = what you change; dependent = what you measure; control = what you keep the same. A fair test changes only one variable.
Prediction = "I predict … because …" (use science). Conclusion = answer the question + scientific reason + compare with the prediction.
Repeat measurements and take the mean to make results reliable; leave anomalous results out of the mean.
Bar chart for categories, line graph for numbers, scatter graph for pattern seeking (points not joined), dot plot for how often each value appears.
Read scales carefully (value of one small division, eye level) and always write the unit: mass in g or kg, weight in N, temperature in °C.
Improvement = what to change + why it helps.
